concepts.title: Price as Quality Badge
concepts.excerpt: The same wine at £5 vs. £45: taste difference is imperceptible to blind tasting, but perception of quality differs dramatically.

concepts.title: Price Relativity
concepts.excerpt: A product costs £50. Is that expensive or cheap? The answer depends entirely on context.

concepts.title: Charm Pricing
concepts.excerpt: A product priced at $4. 99 sells 9% more units than the identical product at $5.

concepts.title: Temporal Reframing & Pennies-a-Day
concepts.excerpt: A sports car costs £50,000. You can't afford it. A sports car costs £4.

concepts.title: False Scarcity
concepts.excerpt: A soup can has unlimited soup available. Same soup with a sign "Limit 12 per customer": average consumption jumps to 7 cans (25% increase over the control 5.

concepts.title: Sold Out Framing
concepts.excerpt: A product is unavailable. You can frame it as "Out of Stock" or "Sold Out."

concepts.title: Regret Lottery
concepts.excerpt: The Dutch Postcode Lottery model: you buy a ticket, your postal code enters a drawing, and if your postcode is drawn, all residents in that postcode split a prize.

concepts.title: Costly Signaling
concepts.excerpt: This is counterintuitive. You'd think efficiency would be credible. But authenticity has always been costly.

concepts.title: Fluent Devices & Mascots
concepts.excerpt: A gecko speaks in a smooth accent. A lizard selling insurance shouldn't work—insects don't understand risk management.

concepts.title: Foreign Branding
concepts.excerpt: A brand named "Häagen-Dazs" sounds Scandinavian/European, signaling quality and heritage.

concepts.title: Keats Heuristic & Rhyming
concepts.excerpt: A rhyming slogan lodges itself in your brain and refuses to leave. Your brain treats the fluency of rhyme—the ease with which the phrase flows—as evidence that it's true.

concepts.title: Descriptive Language & Word Choice
concepts.excerpt: A car accident is the same event. But describe it as "cars contacted each other" and witnesses estimate impact speed at 31.

concepts.title: Zeigarnik Effect
concepts.excerpt: A magician starts a trick and stops mid-way. You remember the incomplete trick more vividly than a completed trick.

concepts.title: Skeuomorphism
concepts.excerpt: A leather texture wraps around your phone's digital calendar. Your digital notepad sounds like paper tearing when you delete a note.

concepts.title: Synesthesia & Multi-Sensory Branding
concepts.excerpt: A heavy fork in your hand. The food tastes better—objectively better. Not subjectively "feels fancier," but measurably higher satisfaction ratings and willingness-to-pay increases of 10-15%.

concepts.title: Information Gap & Curiosity
concepts.excerpt: Loewenstein (1994) formalized this as information gap theory. Curiosity is not random—it's triggered by specific gaps between what you know and what you want to know.

concepts.title: Averted Gaze
concepts.excerpt: An image of a face looking at the camera pulls your attention to the face.

concepts.title: Stolen Thunder Technique
concepts.excerpt: A product has a flaw. You can hide it, hope competitors don't mention it, or—counterintuitively—mention it first, yourself.

concepts.title: Loss Aversion
concepts.excerpt: Hold £10 in your hand. You've got it. Now someone offers you a choice: keep the £10, or flip a coin—heads you win £20, tails you lose £10.

concepts.title: Scarcity Bias
concepts.excerpt: This is why "limited edition" sells out. It's why real estate agents say "three other offers pending."

concepts.title: Expectation Assimilation
concepts.excerpt: Kraft Cheese understood this ruthlessly. Their product wasn't premium—it was powdered milk turned into slices.
